summary: Discovery to understand Peregrine's current stack (OpenAI + self-hosted vLLM for cost), key constraints around data residency and SSO, and their success criteria for parity. topics: POC next steps and benchmark plan
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-14 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Aisha (Peregrine Head of ML), Tom (Platform Eng), Lina (Security)

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we know youre all super busy so we'll try to be crisp; quick intros?
[00:12] Aisha: hi yeah i'm aisha head of ml at peregrine, i run the ml platform and we own the models in prod, hey tom lina.
[00:18] Tom: tom, infra/platform eng i manage the cluster and deployments.
[00:21] Lina: lina security lead, focused on compliance and keys.
[00:25] Maya: great, diego i'll hand to you to start with a 2 minute where-we-fit overview and then we'll jump into your current setup.
[00:33] Diego: perfect, thanks maya. so redwood provides a unified inference runtime — hosted api, dedicated reserved pools, or a private vpc/on-prem control plane. we focus on predictable latency, batching, kv/prefix caching, and fallback policies so your app keeps running when capacity is tight. we also do model versioning and rollouts.
[00:54] Aisha: yep so our question is mainly around migrating off the mix we have today — we use openai for a lot of prod traffic and we've started self-hosting for costy flows using vllm on prem plus tgi in a cloud couple of spots. getting parity on outputs and latency is the big ask.
[01:15] Diego: makes total sense. quick question on the self-hosted side: are you running vLLM with quantized checkpoints? what's your token distribution/seq length?
[01:25] Tom: we're using q4_v2 checkpoints on vLLM, avg seq length for chat is 320 tokens; some batch jobs hit up to 1,200. we do a mix of synchronous low-latency calls and async bulk generation.
[01:40] Diego: okay that's helpful. vllm + q4 is common, we typically match quant profiles and test for inference parity. do you use TGI for any model families specifically?
[01:49] Aisha: yes for a few optimized rerankers we use TGI on g4 instances. mainline chat and summarization is openai gpt-4 and our fallback on vllm. cost is pushing us to increase the self-hosted share but parity/regressions are scary.
[02:05] Maya: can you say what your acceptable latency SLO is and what cost target you are trying to hit?
[02:11] Aisha: for consumer-facing chat we need p95 under 700ms ideally under 500ms; cost we'd like to cut token cost by ~40% compared to current openai spend but without hurting accuracy.
[02:22] Tom: also we need audit logs and SSO/SAML for all infra. we can't have secrets in shared managed tenants; KMS integration is mandatory.
[02:33] Lina: and data residency, we have EU-only customer data for order histories. private deployment or dedicated in eu region is a requirement for that subset.
[02:43] Diego: okay noted. so there are three vectors: output parity/regressions, latency/cost for your workload shape, and compliance/residency. for parity we usually do a regression harness where we run your prompt set against the source (openai/vllm) and candidate models on redwood, check metrics and diffs. for latency/cost we plug your seq-length distribution into our batching model and run microbenchmarks.
[03:06] Aisha: what about model compatibility — we have a lot of custom tokens and local adapters, do you preserve adapter weights?
[03:14] Diego: adapters and LoRA are typically supported as long as you can export to a transformers-compatible checkpoint; there are edge cases with custom operators but we can work through them in the POC.
[03:26] Maya: quick question on fallbacks — if a dedicated pool is saturated how does redwood degrade?
[03:31] Diego: policy-based routing: you can set priority to route to lower-cost variants, or fallback to hosted api tiers, or use region-remote capacity. we also have automatic canary rollbacks if regressions are detected.
[03:44] Tom: hmm that sounds useful. what about streaming / function-calling parity with openai? some of our client code expects streaming tokens.
[03:52] Diego: we support streaming and function-calling primitives; implementation differs per model backend but we expose the same API semantics. sometimes timestamps in token streaming are slightly off in transcripts, transcription quirks, but functional parity is there.
[04:08] Aisha: can you run an eval that compares openai gpt-4 responses to a local smaller variant and measure semantic similarity? we need to be sure business-critical responses dont regress.
[04:19] Diego: yes — we run eval suites using embedding-based similarity, n-gram and custom checks. we also do guardrail checks per prompt set. if you share a representative prompt corpus we'll build the baseline.
[04:31] Lina: on security, what's your standard for key management? we require a bring-your-own-kms option for private and dedicated.
[04:39] Maya: we offer KMS/HSM integrations for private deployments and customer-managed keys for dedicated; hosted api can use Redwood KMS but you can opt for a VPC-private control plane where keys are customer-owned.
[04:53] Lina: ok and audit retention? we need 12 months of access logs for compliance.
[04:59] Maya: audit logs retention is configurable; for enterprise packages we can retain and export logs for 12 months or longer and integrate with SIEM.
[05:10] Tom: what about model artifacts — we are concerned about model sprawl. can redwood pin model versions and do rollbacks?
[05:16] Diego: yes we provide model versioning, rollout policies, and you can pin specific model artifacts per route. it's part of the console.
[05:25] Aisha: diving back into cost: you mentioned batching and KV/prefix caching. for our use case with repeated user prompts and context reuse, do you support prefix sharing across requests?
[05:35] Diego: yes — we have prefix/KV caching and transparent reuse so repeated prefixes dont re-execute attention. that tends to dramatically reduce per-token compute for chatty workloads.
[05:44] Aisha: interesting. we saw about 30% savings with our first-pass caching but it was brittle. how mature is that in your runtime?
[05:51] Diego: it's stable, but cache hit rates depend on your prompt engineering and session patterns; we'll instrument and share hit-rate dashboards in the POC.
[06:02] Maya: earlier you mentioned tgi; can you clarify if redwood will run TGI bundles or do you convert to a common runtime?
[06:10] Diego: we can run TGI where it makes sense but the typical approach is to ingest model artifacts into our runtime (we support torch/transformers checkpoints) and ensure kernel selection/quant pipelines match. sometimes customers prefer running TGI for specific workloads — we're flexible.
[06:27] Tom: do you have any customers who've moved from a vllm+openai hybrid to redwood and kept costs down? any case studies?
[06:35] Maya: yes, we've got a retailer and a fintech that reduced hosted token spend by 40% and improved p95 by 20% by moving to dedicated pools and tuning batching and caching. i'll share anonymized notes after.
[06:47] Aisha: great. can we talk about the POC scope? i'd like us to focus first on core parity and p95 latency for the chat path, then a secondary test for bulk generation.
[06:58] Diego: recommended POC: 1) run your prompt suite across openai baseline, your vLLM setup, and a Redwood candidate; 2) run latency/throughput microbenchmarks using your seq distribution on a dedicated pool; 3) exercise security integration (SSO + KMS) in a private sandbox if needed. that should be 2-3 weeks.
[07:20] Tom: timeline wise we're aiming to choose a vendor within 6 weeks and start a pilot at the end of Q3.
[07:27] Maya: sounds doable. Lina any blockers from security side for a private sandbox?
[07:32] Lina: we need a written data flow and assurances that keys never leave our control for private. for hosted we will not push EU data. also need encryption in transit and at rest details.
[07:44] Diego: we'll put together a security pack with architecture diagrams and KMS options.
[07:49] Aisha: one more technical point — our platform uses custom tokenizers and a couple of private vocab merges. will that break if we change runtimes?
[07:58] Diego: custom tokenizers can be loaded as part of the model artifact; we do validation in the onboarding to ensure token-id mappings are preserved. there are occasional mismatches with special unicode sequences but we handle mapping layers.
[08:14] Tom: on the infra side, what networking models do you support for private? VPC peering, transit gateway?
[08:21] Maya: for private we support customer VPC peering, transit gateway, and on-prem connectivity via secure tunnels; we can map to your existing networking.
[08:31] Lina: legal question — do you support data deletion requests and can you prove deletion for a model trained or fine-tuned with customer data?
[08:40] Diego: deletion is supported for artifacts and logs; for fine-tuning it's more complex, we support removing checkpoints and can recreate models without the data — we'll document the process and provide verification steps.
[08:52] Aisha: reasonable. ok i'd like to outline the benchmark: we'll share a 500-prompt subset representing heavy and light chatter, the full token distribution, and a couple of reranker tasks. can you provide the spreadsheet template?
[09:04] Diego: yes i'll share the spreadsheet, columns for prompt, expected baseline, metrics to capture (embedding sim, rouge, mean opinion score if you have human labels), latency p50/p95, token counts, and cost per call.
[09:18] Maya: logistics — i'll send the SOC2 and compliance pack and an initial commercial quoter for hosted vs dedicated vs private options.
[09:27] Tom: on pricing, high level, how do you price dedicated vs hosted? is there a commit or is it usage-based?
[09:34] Maya: hosted is pay-as-you-go; dedicated is a reserved capacity with monthly/annual commit options that lowers unit cost. private has a platform/license fee and support add-ons. we'll share example scenarios.
[09:45] Aisha: one operational question: how do rollouts work if we want to A/B test a candidate? do you support canary percentages?
[09:52] Diego: yes, console supports canary rollouts, traffic splitting by route, and auto-fallback if error rates rise.
[09:59] Lina: about SSO — we use Okta. can we do SAML SSO for the console and role-based access?
[10:06] Maya: yes Okta SAML is supported and RBAC is configurable per team.
[10:11] Aisha: great. any performance gotchas we should watch when moving from vLLM to your runtime?
[10:17] Diego: two common gotchas: 1) kernel selection/quantization mismatches causing small output diffs, and 2) batching configurations that are too aggressive hurting tail latency for sync calls. we tune per workload and recommend iterations.
[10:31] Tom: will you run a small perf validation on our vLLM artifacts as-is?
[10:36] Diego: yes we can accept model artifacts and run a compatibility check and microbenchmarks. we'll need a sample docker or a snapshot of your vllm config and weights access.
[10:48] Aisha: is there any proprietary telemetry you collect? our legal team is concerned about customer data exposure.
[10:55] Maya: telemetry is operational (latency, errors, token counts) and we redact prompt content in hosted unless you opt-in; in private deployments telemetry stays in your control. we'll include data handling policies in the security pack.
[11:09] Tom: final question — what does success look like for you in the POC? faster p95, within tolerance for semantic similarity, and a path to cost parity.
[11:18] Diego: absolutely, those are good measurable criteria. we'll put together an evaluation rubric.
[11:25] Maya: ok let's recap next steps: maya to send security/commercial, diego share benchmark template and runbook, tom to provide vllm config and sample prompts, schedule POC kickoff next week. anyone object?
[11:39] Aisha: all good. thanks everyone.
[11:42] Lina: thank you.
[11:44] Maya: thanks team, we'll follow up with calendar invites and docs. bye.

Notes: transcript contains minor transcription artifacts; speaker turns approximate. Shared artifacts referenced: security pack (link shared in follow-up), benchmark spreadsheet template (to be sent), anonymized case study.
